name: The Kingdom of Heaven / concrete other-worldliness
plain_explanation: Unlike Greek philosophers, who imagined a timeless, purely intellectual 'real' world behind the world of appearances, Jews and Christians imagined a literal future world -- a future time when the good will be rewarded and the wicked punished.
precise_definition: The Jewish and Christian doctrine that the 'Other World' is not metaphysically different from this world but lies in the future, when the virtuous will enjoy everlasting bliss and the wicked will suffer everlasting torment -- a concrete, temporal other-worldliness rather than the Greek philosophers' atemporal metaphysical one.
why_it_mattered: Russell argues this concrete, revenge-inflected doctrine was 'intelligible to all and sundry,' unlike the abstract doctrines of Greek philosophers, and this popular intelligibility helped Christianity spread.
historical_origin: A Jewish elaboration of older Near Eastern and Persian-influenced ideas about an afterlife, sharpened during persecution.
examples: The Book of Enoch's vivid descriptions of heaven, hell, and the Last Judgement
competing_positions: Platonic doctrine that the sensible world in space and time is illusion and that the eternal, non-temporal world alone is real
influence_on_later_thinkers: Shapes popular Christian eschatology throughout the Middle Ages, as distinct from more Platonized theological Christianity.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Religious doctrine with an emotional root Russell calls 'revenge psychology.'
